drills.q: True or false: trunk-based development means committing directly to main with no branches at all.
drills.a: False -- it means short-lived branches (under ~24h) merged into main at least daily, with incomplete work hidden behind feature flags, not zero branching.

drills.q: Name the three prerequisites for trunk-based development to work in practice, not just in name.
drills.a: Fast/reliable CI, a merge queue, and feature-flag discipline.

drills.q: Which IDE shipped native git worktree UI in its 2026.1 release?
Two PRs each pass CI independently, merge back-to-back, and main breaks even though neither PR's own CI run showed a problem. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: No merge queue -- each PR was tested against main-at-branch-time, not the actual resulting state after the other PR landed. Fix: adopt a merge queue that serially re-tests each PR against the real current main before it merges.

drills.q: Explain why squash-merge is bisect-friendly and what it costs.
drills.a: Every commit on main becomes atomic and independently testable, so bisect's binary search converges on a coherent state every time. It costs the true intra-feature development history -- false starts and fine-grained fix commits collapse into one commit.

drills.q: Why does a single shared git checkout break down when running several AI coding agents against one repo concurrently?
drills.a: All agents share one working directory and index -- one agent's file write can be read mid-edit by another, git status becomes meaningless with concurrent changes, and there's real lock contention on the index. A worktree per agent isolates the working directory and index while sharing one object database.

drills.q: What does a git worktree NOT automatically duplicate when you create one, and why does this matter for agent setups?
drills.a: Untracked local state, like .env files -- worktree only clones git-tracked content. Each new agent worktree needs untracked config copied in explicitly, or its dev environment silently uses stale/missing config.

drills.q: Why is rebasing an already-shared, pushed branch categorically different from rebasing your own unpushed local branch?
drills.a: Rebase produces new commit SHAs (same tree, different parent). On a pushed branch others have pulled, this creates a genuinely diverged history with no shared ancestor at those points for them -- their next pull duplicates commits or fails. On your own unpushed branch, there's no shared state to diverge, so it's safe to rebase freely.

drills.q: A team's git bisect results have been unreliable for months and nobody trusts them. What do you check first, and what's the actual root-cause fix versus the per-instance rescue?
drills.a: Check whether branching topology has drifted from trunk-based into long-lived branches with merge commits, which breaks bisect's linearity assumption -- this is the most common root cause. Per-instance rescue: rebase a suspect range onto a synthetic linear line before bisecting it. Root-cause fix: restore genuinely short-lived branches and consistent squash-merging so every FUTURE bisect is reliable without rescue.

drills.q: Design the branching workflow for 40 engineers plus a dozen AI agents working against one repo, avoiding both merge chaos and agent-collision chaos.
drills.a: Trunk-based with all three prerequisites (fast CI, merge queue, feature flags) for the shared branching strategy. Each AI agent gets its own git worktree on its own short-lived branch, sharing the team's single object database, integrating through the SAME merge-queue-and-flag pipeline as human work. Branch-age limits in CI catch both humans and agents drifting long. Squash-merge given the volume of agent commits that would otherwise clutter main's history.

drills.q: A team resists shortening feature branches, arguing 'our features are just bigger than a day of work.' What's the actual gap this argument is masking?
drills.a: Usually a feature-flag gap wearing a branch-lifetime costume -- a large feature can still merge incrementally, dark behind a flag, in small daily pieces, flipped on only when complete. 'The feature is big' argues for flagging, not for a long branch; conflating the two produces trunk-based-in-name-only.
